_comment: Hindu expansion 175-drive P: final batch (Griffith 1870-74; Ganguli 1883-96; Wilson 1840; Eggeling 1885; Mackenzie 1913), public domain.

title.en: Kama Burned by the Third Eye

texts.period: Puranic cycle, retold in Donald A. Mackenzie, Indian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. VIII (public domain)

source.work: Indian Myth and Legend, by Donald A. Mackenzie (1913), ch. VIII

summary.en: The gods needed Shiva married to Parvati to get a general against the demons - and the ascetic god would not look at her. They sent Kama, god of love, with his flower bow; one arrow found Shiva in meditation, and the god's third eye opened and burned the archer to ash. Desire died for the mission; Rati the wife's mourning earned his restoration as 'the bodiless one', Ananga - love that lives without a body.
summary.zh: 諸神需要濕婆娶波羅婆蒂以得對抗群魔的統帥——而苦行的神不肯看她。他們派出愛神伽摩執花弓；一箭射中禪定中的濕婆，神之第三眼開而將射手焚為灰燼。欲望為使命而死；其妻臘底的哀哭換來他以『無身者』（Ananga）復原——無形而活的愛。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Holi's Kamadeva burning); source is a public-domain scholarly retelling; recorded as such. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The plot was the gods' generalship: a demon-army needed a son of Shiva, and the only obstacle was Shiva's vow of not-looking - so they sent the one arrow that could make him look.
passages.note: Retold from Mackenzie, Indian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: The flower-bow found its mark; the meditation broke for a heartbeat - and the third eye, the god's alarm system, incinerated the intruder where he stood.
passages.note: Retold from Mackenzie, Indian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Rati's grief argued the case in heaven: love without a body is still love - and the god was restored as Ananga, the bodiless; desire survives its own executions, which is the myth's whole point.
passages.note: Retold from Mackenzie, Indian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. VIII; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Retold in English by Donald A. Mackenzie, 1913 (public domain)

region.zh: 楞伽無憂林苑（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Sundara Kanda, the Ashoka grove

summary.en: In the grove of the Ashoka trees, Sita sat captive under guard - and Ravana came to court her with an empire: be my queen, he said, and the city is yours. She set a blade of grass between them and answered him in a dead level voice: my husband is coming, and your city will not survive the invitation. Her endurance in that grove is the epic's image of constancy.
summary.zh: 在無憂樹之苑中，悉多於看守下靜坐——羅波那前來以帝國求婚：作我的王后，他說，此城即屬於你。她於二人之間放下一根草葉，以平直如死的聲音回答：我的丈夫正在前來，而你的城市經不起這個邀請。她在苑中的堅忍是史詩恆常之德的意象。

passages.text: The grove was a gilded prison: fruit and fountains, demoness guards in shifts, and a woman with one sentence on repeat - Rama is coming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ravana's proposal came in state: jewels, thrones, a co-kingdom - and her answer was the grass-blade held between them, the smallest wall ever drawn, and her voice refusing without raising.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: The threat she named was the epic's own forecast: your city will not outlive my husband's arrival - and the monkey in the tree above heard it as a battle-plan confirmed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.en: The Niyoga: Vyasa Fathers the Age's Two Armies
title.zh: 尼由伽：毗耶娑為時代兩軍之父

texts.period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the births of Dhritarashtra and Pandu

summary.en: With both princes dead and the dynasty heirless, the widows were given to Vyasa under the law of niyoga. Ambika closed her eyes and bore the blind Dhritarashtra; Ambalika turned pale and bore the pale Pandu; the maid, unafraid, bore the wise Vidura. Three looks, three natures, two armies - the epic's genealogy is a psychology experiment conducted in one afternoon.
summary.zh: 二王俱亡而王朝無嗣之際，依尼由伽之法，寡婦被交予毗耶娑。安比迦閉目而生盲眼持國；安波利迦面色轉白而生蒼白般度；侍女無懼而生睿智維杜羅。三種神色、三種天性、兩支大軍——史詩的譜系是一場於一個下午完成的心理實驗。

passages.text: The succession was carried by visitation: the old seer came when called, and each widow's single meeting wrote the next generation's body and temperament.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The closed eyes made the blind king; the pale face made the pale one; the maid's unflinching gaze made the wisest man of the age - looks as fate, recorded in the family's ledger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two armies of Kurukshetra are, by this genealogy, one seer's afternoon: the epic's own way of saying that the war's sides were always one family's nerves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

title.en: Gandhari's Hundred Sons in the Jar

texts.period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the birth of the Kauravas

summary.en: Gandhari, pregnant for two years with a hundred-son blessing gone wrong, struck her iron-hard womb in rage - and delivered a single ball of flesh. Vyasa divided it into a hundred and one jars of ghee; from the first jar came Duryodhana, howling like a jackal at birth; the last, on schedule, was the girl Duhsala. The Kaurava legion was born from one fruit split into vessels.
summary.zh: 甘陀利懷著一項出錯的百子之福達兩年，怒擊其鐵般堅硬的子宮——產下一枚血肉之球。毗耶娑將其分入一百零一罐酥油；自第一罐生出的難敵出生時如豺狼般嚎叫；最後一罐依時而生者為女兒杜莎拉。俱盧軍團誕生於一枚被分割入器的果實。

passages.text: The pregnancy that outlasted the year was a curse in slow motion: one ball of flesh where a hundred sons had been promised - the queen's blow made it worse, and Vyasa was sent for.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The ball was divided with the care of a butcher-scholar: a hundred and one jars, ghee-cooled, each a cradle - the war's personnel grown in pantry vessels.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The first-born's omen - howling like a jackal on the night of his birth - was reported to the king, and the king heard it as weather; the epic records the omen as the age's opening invoice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

title.zh: 日落時分的闍耶陀羅陀之首

texts.period: Mahabharata, Drona Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Drona Parva, Jayadratha-vadha

summary.en: Jayadratha had held the gate against the Pandava rescuers while Abhimanyu died - Arjuna's vow: your head will leave your shoulders before tomorrow's sunset or I will burn myself. On the fourteenth day the sun went down and the vow had failed - until Krishna obscured the light: the fool raised his head in triumph at false sunset, the arrows flew, and the head was carried by the arrow to fall in his father's lap - a curse fulfilled twice.
summary.zh: 闍耶陀羅陀曾在阿毗曼紐死時守住營門抵抗般度救援軍——阿周那立誓：明日日落之前你的頭顱必離其肩，否則我自焚。第十四日，太陽落下而誓言已敗——直到克里希那遮蔽天光：那愚者在假日落時仰首慶賀，箭矢飛出，頭顱被箭攜至其父之膝落下——一個詛咒應驗兩次。

passages.text: The vow was the war's most specific: one head, one sunset, one self-immolation - the kind of contract the field took as ordinary.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sunset arrived without the head; the archer drew for the pyre - and the light broke: a cloud made by a god gave the day a second evening.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The false dusk brought the head up, the true arrows brought it down, and the father's curse (that it fall in his lap) closed like a latch - the epic's most surgical revenge, on schedule.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

title.en: The Epic's Frame: Vyasa, Vaishampayana and the Snake Sacrifice
title.zh: 史詩框架：毗耶娑、婆藪仙般耶那與蛇祭

region.zh: 怛叉始羅，祭祀之堂（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Parvasangraha), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the recitation frame

summary.en: The epic tells us how it was made: Vyasa composed it; his pupil Vaishampayana recited it first at Janamejaya's snake-sacrifice, to the grandson of the story's own heroes; sages collected it in the Naimisha forest from Ugrashravas the wandering bard. The Mahabharata builds its own reception history into its first book - a text about its own telling.
summary.zh: 史詩自述其成書：毗耶娑構作之；其弟子婆藪仙般耶那首於闍那彌覺耶的蛇祭上誦之，聽眾正是故事主角的曾孫；仙人們於尼彌沙林自雲遊詠者鄔伽什羅婆娑集之。《摩訶婆羅多》將自身的接受史寫入首卷——一部講述自身如何被講述的文本。

passages.text: The chain of telling is the epic's first content: Vyasa composed; the pupil recited at the sacrifice; the bard carried it to the forest assembly - authorship as relay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The audience is inside the story: the king listening at the snake-sacrifice is the great-grandson of the heroes whose deaths the poem is already mourning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The frame makes the text its own archive: every recitation the reader imagines is one more link in the chain the first book lists - reception history as a genre.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

region.en: Cosmic ocean, churning site (symbolic pin at Kailasa)
region.zh: 宇宙之海，攪海之地（象徵性定位於吉羅娑）

texts.period: Puranic cycle (Vishnu Purana, Book I, ch. 9; Bhagavata 8.7 tradition), c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, the churning and the poison (with Bhagavata tradition)

summary.en: In the Purana's churning, the first thing the ocean gave up was poison - halahala, black as midnight, hot enough to burn the three worlds. The gods fled to Shiva, who drank the world's poison down and held it in his throat; his neck turned blue, and the goddess pressed her hand there to stop it spreading. The blue-throated god is the cosmos' poison-sink: Nilakantha.
summary.zh: 往世書的攪海中，海洋吐出的第一物即是毒——黑如午夜、熱可焚三界的哈拉哈拉。諸神逃至濕婆，他將世界之毒一飲而盡，將其鎖於喉中；其頸轉為青色，女神以手按其喉以阻其擴散。青頸之神是宇宙的毒之受納者：尼羅迦陀。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Shivaratri, Nilakantha imagery); classified 'myth'. Purana locus for the poison episode varies by recension - noted.

passages.text: The first yield of the churning was not treasure but waste: a poison that darkened the sky and began to eat the worlds - the ocean's wages paid before its gifts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book I (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: Shiva drank it as a drain takes a flood: the god held the whole dose in his throat, and the throat's blue is the receipt - Nilakantha, the blue-necked one, marked forever by service.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book I (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: The goddess's hand at his throat is the myth's tenderness: the poison is contained by a grip - the world's survival maintained by a wife's palm on her husband's neck.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book I (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

title.en: Building the Fire-Altar: Agni's Body of Bricks
title.zh: 築火壇：磚砌的阿耆尼之身

region.zh: 俱盧-般遮羅祭地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Shatapatha Brahmana 6-10, c. 8th-6th c. BCE (Eggeling translation, 1882-85)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East)
source.work: The Satapatha-Brahmana, trans. Julius Eggeling (SBE 41, 1885), the agnichayana chapters

summary.en: The Brahmana's grandest construction myth: the fire-altar is built as a person, in five layers of a thousand bricks, each brick named, each layer a world - earth, air, heaven and two between. The builder is rebuilding Agni's body (the god whose head was lost); when the five layers stand, the sacrificer climbs them to heaven's gate. Architecture as resurrection manual.
summary.zh: 梵書最宏大的營造神話：火壇以五層千磚築成一人之形，每一磚皆有名，每一層即一個世界——地、空、天與其間二者。築者是在重建阿耆尼之身（失去頭顱的神）；五層既成，祭者登之，直達天門。建築即復活手冊。

passages.text: The altar is a man made of masonry: five layers, a thousand bricks, each brick with a name and a verse - the sacrificed god rebuilt by contractors of ritual.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana, agnichayana chapters (Eggeling 1885); not verbatim.

passages.text: The layers are the worlds in order: earth the base, air the middle, heaven the crown, with the transitional courses between - a skyline drawn as theology.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana, agnichayana chapters (Eggeling 1885); not verbatim.

passages.text: The climax is structural: on the finished altar the sacrificer is lifted - the building's purpose is a doorway, and masonry is the road the dead man's body takes upward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana, agnichayana chapters (Eggeling 1885); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pact of Rama and Sugriva

region.zh: 黎沙牟迦山（象徵性定位於漢皮）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Kishkindha Kanda, the alliance

summary.en: Two exiles made each other's wars their own: Rama would kill Vali for the throne; Sugriva would turn the monkey nations out for the search. The fire-pact was sworn at the hill - and the four directions were then dispatched as search parties, each named, each a catalogue of the world's monkey-tribes. The alliance is the epic's diplomatic charter: personal debt transmuted into a coalition.
summary.zh: 兩位流亡者將彼此的戰爭化為己任：羅摩為猴王之位誅婆黎；須羯哩婆則為搜索傾盡猴國之力。火前立盟於山巔——四方隨即被派作搜索隊，各有其名，各為一份世界猴族之清單。此盟是史詩的外交憲章：私人恩義化為聯軍。

passages.text: The pact was struck like a treaty between states: one arrow for a throne, one army for a search - both parties investing their own blood in the other's cause.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fire was witness, and the dispatch orders that followed read like a census: north, east, west and south, each monkey-nation named and pointed at the horizon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: The south-party found the quarry because its commander was the one monkey who could leap the sea - the alliance's return on investment measured in one flight to Lanka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.
